source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on supporting novice learners in introductory programming
finding: Matched-groups controlled study: novices with Codex wrote far better code during training, but did not do better on later manual tests.
numbers: 69 learners aged 10-17, 45 Python authoring tasks, 33 Codex vs 36 baseline (after 21 dropped). Training authoring correctness Codex 80.1% vs 44.4% (d=1.67); completion time much shorter (d=1.56); modifying tasks 66.2% vs 58.4% (d=0.31, n.s.).
limits: Short camp, ages 10-17, Scratch pre-training, lab setting; Codex 2022 era.
agent_relevance: Gains on the task are not gains in the learner. Judge help by retained skill, not by task output.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on supporting novice learners in introductory programming
finding: Immediate post-test (1 day later) showed no group difference; one-week retention test showed a small edge for the Codex group, mainly for those with high prior skill.
numbers: Immediate authoring 61.3% vs 62.9% (d=0.05); modifying 59.7% vs 59.3% (d=0.01). Retention authoring 59.1% vs 49.8% (d=0.28, p=.262); modifying 47.5% vs 34.8% (d=0.41, p=.092). Codex-High did significantly better than Baseline-High on several retention measures; Codex-Low vs Baseline-Low near equal.
limits: Subgroup split by pre-test (n about 16-18 per cell); retention gains partly not significant.
agent_relevance: Aid helps strong users more than weak ones (Matthew effect); expect the same for an agent scaffold.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on supporting novice learners in introductory programming
finding: Learners with Codex leaned less on documentation and made fewer syntax errors, and mostly pasted the task text as the prompt.
numbers: Doc access 22.1% vs 54.3% of authoring tasks (d=1.33); syntax errors 0.87 vs 1.67 per task (d=0.88); 32% of 1646 prompts identical to task description; AI code used unmodified in 49% of tasks.
agent_relevance: Tool shifts effort from syntax to checking; copy-the-spec prompting is the default failure.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The Widening Gap: benefits and harms of generative AI for novice programmers
finding: Replication of Prather 2020 lab study (n=31) with GenAI added. All old novice metacognitive difficulties persisted and some were compounded; a divide appeared between students who accelerated and those who struggled.
numbers: 21 CS1 students (27 enrolled, 21 opted in), eye tracking plus think-aloud. 20 of 21 finished. 10 struggled; 9 of those used GenAI to reach a solution. Original study: 11 of 31 did not finish in time.
limits: Small n, one institution, one problem, qualitative coding.
agent_relevance: Struggling users with a strong tool show false confidence. Scaffold should force self-checking, not just supply code.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The Widening Gap: benefits and harms of generative AI for novice programmers
finding: Struggling students expressed an illusion of competence: they thought they did better than they did after leaning on GenAI output.
numbers: Observed in the struggling group (10 of 21); accelerating students ignored unhelpful inline suggestions and used AI for code they already intended.
quote: Students who accelerated created code they already intended to make
limits: Self-report plus observation; no preregistered effect size.
agent_relevance: Expertise decides whether suggestions help. Confidence reports after AI assistance are unreliable.

source: Berger et al. (2019) On the impact of programming languages on code quality: a reproduction study
finding: Reproduction of Ray et al. (FSE 2014, language vs defects on GitHub). Repetition only partly worked; reanalysis found far weaker support: only 4 of 11 languages kept a significant link to defects, and effects were tiny.
numbers: Original: 729 projects, 17 languages, 1.5M commits, 566k bug-fix commits, 29k authors. Reanalysis: 148 extra projects found, 27,450 duplicate commits (1.86%) removed, false positive rate of bug labels 36%, false negative 11%. Significant languages 11 down to 4.
quote: only four languages are found to have a statistically significant association with defects
limits: Observational data, no causal claim possible; commit-message bug labelling is noisy.
agent_relevance: Famous 'typed functional languages mean fewer bugs' claim does not survive clean analysis.

source: Berger et al. (2019) On the impact of programming languages on code quality: a reproduction study
finding: The original claimed association with a small effect, but its readers and even citing authors often restated it as a causal language effect.
numbers: Authors surveyed papers citing the original and reported many treated it as causation.
agent_relevance: Do not let our agent cite a language-effect claim without checking its replication status.

source: Becker et al. (METR, 2025) Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developer productivity
finding: RCT on real work by experienced developers: allowing AI made tasks take longer, even though developers believed it sped them up.
numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks (avg 2.0 h), mature repos with 5 yrs average prior experience; AI allowed = +19% completion time. Forecast before: -24%; belief after: -20%. Economists forecast -39%, ML experts -38%. Only 44% had prior Cursor experience.
limits: Small n of developers, 2025 tools (Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7), highly familiar large repos; authors say effects may differ elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Perceived and measured speed-up can have opposite sign; log time and acceptance, not feelings.

source: Becker et al. (METR, 2025) Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developer productivity
finding: Time-use analysis: with AI, developers spent less time actively coding and searching, and more time prompting, waiting on and reviewing AI output, and idle.
numbers: 143 hours of screen recordings labelled (128 recordings); 74 recordings (84 h) kept after filtering. 21 candidate factors checked.
agent_relevance: Cost of verification is where gains vanish; argues for cheap checking steps.

source: Peng et al. (2023) The impact of AI on developer productivity: evidence from GitHub Copilot
finding: Controlled experiment with Copilot on one standard task: treated group was much faster.
numbers: 95 Upwork professionals, write an HTTP server in JavaScript. Mean 71.17 min treated vs 160.89 control = 55.8% faster (95% CI 21-89%, p=0.0017). Success rate difference not significant (CI -0.11 to 0.25). Both groups guessed 35% productivity gain.
limits: Single self-contained greenfield task, 2022, four outliers noted.
agent_relevance: Contrast with METR: greenfield small task gives big gain, familiar large repo gives slowdown. Task type is the moderator.

source: Peng et al. (2023) The impact of AI on developer productivity: evidence from GitHub Copilot
finding: Heterogeneous effects: less experienced, older, and higher hours-per-day programmers gained most.
numbers: Interaction table: hours of programming per day coefficient 78.01 (SE 67.84, p=.26); income under $20,000 -74.55 (SE 33.52, p=0.03).
agent_relevance: Novice benefit here conflicts with the Matthew-effect reading in education studies; moderator depends on outcome (speed vs learning).

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp: LLMs with guardrails for scalable support in programming classes
finding: Guardrailed LLM help (does not give full solutions) deployed in a 12-week first-year course; students used it steadily and rated it useful.
numbers: 52 students enrolled, 49 analysed; about 70% used it in 4+ weeks; about 80% sent 10+ queries; 7 of 49 sent over 100 (one over 600); 45 survey responses; 71% agreed it helped complete work.
limits: No control group, self-report only, instructor reflections, one course.
agent_relevance: Guardrail by prompt pipeline is a workable pattern; effect on learning not measured.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp
finding: Open-text complaints: 14 students said it is hard to use when you do not understand the problem; 5 said it used constructs not yet taught.
numbers: Counts from 45 survey responses; students also said it never handed over the answer.
agent_relevance: Help quality depends on user's ability to state the problem; a scaffold may need to elicit it.

source: Denny et al. (2023) Prompt Problems: a new programming exercise for the generative AI era
finding: New exercise type: students write a prompt so an LLM produces code that passes tests. Deployed first time in CS1 and CS2 with a tool, Promptly.
numbers: Share of attempting students who solved each problem: CS1-1 76%, CS1-2 86%, CS1-3 65%, CS2-1 75%, CS2-2 96%, CS2-3 99%; mean 1.3-7.5 submissions; successful prompts averaged 18-47.9 words.
limits: Descriptive only, no learning outcome versus a control.
agent_relevance: Prompting is a teachable skill; success is high when tests are visible.

source: Becker et al. (2022) Programming is hard, or at least it used to be
finding: Position paper reviewing early Codex and AlphaCode results for education.
numbers: Codex solved 29% of HumanEval problems at one sample, 70% with repeated sampling; Codex beat almost 80% of students on CS1 exam questions (Finnie-Ansley); AlphaCode top 54% of 5,000+ Codeforces entrants; 11% of its Python solutions raised SyntaxError, 35% of C++ did not compile.
limits: Secondary reporting of other studies; early models.
agent_relevance: Shows how fast the capability ceiling moved; old numbers are stale.

source: Denny et al. (2023) Computing education in the era of generative AI
finding: Review of LLM performance on CS1 tasks and uses in teaching: Codex scored about 78% on two exams, and generated exercises were mostly usable.
numbers: Codex 15.7/20 (78.5%) Exam 1, 19.5/25 (78.0%) Exam 2. Generated exercises: about 80% novel; 84.6% had sample solution; 70.8% passed all tests; 30.9% reached full statement coverage; code explanations 90% covered all parts.
limits: Mix of authors' own studies on a 2021-22 model.
agent_relevance: Quality gates (tests, coverage) separated usable outputs; supports a check step.

source: Sarkar et al. (2022) What is it like to program with artificial intelligence?
finding: Review of usability studies and reports: LLM-assisted programming differs from compilation, pair programming and search; main costs are prompt framing and checking or debugging output.
numbers: Notes prior lab and telemetry studies show developers like these tools despite no strong effect on completion time or correctness.
agent_relevance: Work shifts from writing to checking; design the scaffold around verification.

source: Margulieux et al. (2024) as cited in Prather et al. 2024
finding: Second-hand via Prather: students' GenAI use correlated with lower grades, lower self-efficacy and higher fear of failure; may mean help reaches those who need it, or harms them.
numbers: Correlational; no numbers in the citing text.
agent_relevance: Use of the aid signals struggle; not proof of harm.

source: Loksa et al. (2016) as cited in Prather et al. 2024
finding: Second-hand via Prather: telling novices which of six problem-solving stages they are in raised performance.
numbers: Six stages: reinterpret prompt, search analogous problems, search solutions, evaluate solution, implement, evaluate implemented solution. No effect size in citing text.
agent_relevance: Stage-awareness prompts have education support; our schema states play a similar role.

source: Stefik and Siebert (2013) An empirical investigation into programming language syntax
finding: Randomised novice study of syntax. From memory, some popular syntaxes did not beat a random syntax in novice accuracy. Not opened; web search budget was exhausted.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Syntax choice for novices lacks solid evidence.

source: Hanenberg (2010) An experiment about static and dynamic type systems
finding: Controlled experiment on static typing and development time; from memory showed no clear benefit. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Type-system benefit claims are weaker than folklore.

source: Uesbeck, Stefik et al. (2016) An empirical study on the impact of C++ lambdas and programmer experience
finding: Randomised study; from memory lambdas did not help and experience was the strongest factor. Not opened.
numbers: Numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Fancy features may not help; experience dominates.

source: Pea (1986) Language-independent conceptual bugs in novice programming
finding: Classic: novice bugs come from a superbug of assuming the computer understands intent like a human, not from syntax. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Mirrors LLM habit of assuming intent.

source: Sajaniemi roles of variables literature
finding: Teaching aids such as roles of variables show small context-bound gains; replication thin (recalled). Not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Teaching aids give modest gains.

source: Prather et al. (2024) Widening Gap, related work on Copilot productivity
finding: Related work states Copilot raised professional productivity in one RCT while another lab study found no change in time on task, though users preferred it.
numbers: Cites a 55.8% faster result versus a no-time-effect study; adds no numbers.
agent_relevance: Mixed field evidence; do not assume speed gains.
